summary: BIER is a new architecture for forwarding multicast packets. A packet is marked at the ingress router with the set of destinations, and routers forward it without building multicast trees or keeping per-flow state. This document describes the architecture.

plainLanguage.summary:
BIER is a new way to forward multicast traffic. Instead of building a tree and remembering every flow that crosses it, the router where the packet enters writes the list of destination routers into the packet itself, one bit for each router.

Every router along the way reads those bits, copies the packet once for each neighbouring router that leads towards a destination, and clears the bits that do not belong to that copy. The result is that no router in the middle has to remember anything about the flow, and no tree has to be built.

subtitle: Multicast forwarding that writes the destination set into the packet header.

tldr.problem: Ordinary IP multicast needs a protocol that builds distribution trees, and every router on a tree has to keep state for every flow that crosses it. Both cost memory and complicate convergence.
tldr.mechanism: BIER gives each router a small number inside the domain and writes the destination set into the packet as a bit string. A router that receives the packet reads the bits, works out which neighbouring router leads towards each destination, and copies the packet once per neighbour with the relevant bits left set.
tldr.outcome: Routers on the path hold no per-flow state and run no tree-building protocol, and the packet follows the same path as unicast traffic to each destination. The cost is a new addressing scheme that has to be provisioned and kept collision free.

today: RFC 8279 was published in November 2017. The document describes itself as an Experimental specification, published for examination and experimental implementation, while the index on this site lists its status as a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Multicast Without Trees or Per-Flow State
sections.content:
This document specifies a new architecture for forwarding multicast data packets. It gives optimal forwarding through a multicast domain, but it does not require a protocol for explicitly building multicast distribution trees, and it does not require intermediate nodes to maintain any per-flow state. The architecture is called Bit Index Explicit Replication.

A router that supports BIER is called a Bit-Forwarding Router, or BFR. The control-plane protocols run within a BIER domain so that the BFRs in it can exchange what they need in order to forward packets to each other. A multicast data packet enters a BIER domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router and leaves at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers. A BFR that receives a packet from another BFR and forwards it to another BFR is a transit BFR for that packet. One router can be the ingress for some traffic, the egress for other traffic and a transit router for other traffic, and for a single packet it can be any combination of the three.

When a multicast packet arrives from outside the domain at the ingress router, that router determines the set of egress routers the packet must reach, and also determines the sub-domain it will travel in. Assigning a packet to a sub-domain is how that decision is named; the procedures for choosing a sub-domain are outside the scope of the document. Once a packet has been assigned to a sub-domain it stays there until it leaves the domain, so the sub-domain must not change while the packet is in flight.

The ingress router then encapsulates the packet in a BIER header. The header contains a bit string in which each bit stands for exactly one egress router in the domain. To send the packet to a given egress router, the bit for that router is set. The bit string field is called the BitString, and the packet inside is called the payload, so a BIER-encapsulated packet is a BIER header followed by a payload.

The number of destinations a packet can reach is limited only by the length of the BitString, and different deployments may use different lengths. When a sub-domain has more egress routers than the BitString has bits, the encapsulation also carries a Set Identifier. Together the BitString and the Set Identifier decide the destinations: by convention the rightmost bit is bit 1 and the leftmost is bit BitStringLength, and a packet with a Set Identifier of n and bit k set goes to the router whose number is n times BitStringLength plus k. The example in the RFC uses a BitStringLength of 256, and a packet that must reach the routers numbered 13, 126 and 235 is sent with a Set Identifier of zero and those three bits set; a router numbered 257 needs a second copy of the packet with a Set Identifier of 1 and bit 1 set.

Because the set of destinations is written into the header, a packet is never sent to a router that does not need it, and each router can follow an optimal path to each of its destinations. All of this is achieved without transit routers keeping per-flow state or running a multicast tree-building protocol. The number of lookups needed in the forwarding path for one packet is limited to the number of neighbouring BFRs, which can be far smaller than the number of destinations. The RFC notes that the idea of encoding the egress set into a multicast header is not new, but because BIER gives each router a single bit, it can represent up to 128 egress routers in the number of bits it would take to carry one IPv6 address.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual way to send one packet to many receivers is to build a tree and have every router on it remember the traffic. BIER replaces that with a list written into the packet. The list is short and fixed in size, so the routers in between need no memory of the flow at all.

sections.title: BFR Identifiers, Prefixes and Sub-Domains
sections.content:
A BIER domain may contain one or more sub-domains. Every domain must contain at least one, the default sub-domain, also called sub-domain 0. If a domain has more than one, every BFR in it must be provisioned to know which sub-domains it belongs to. Each sub-domain is identified by a sub-domain-id in the range 0 to 255.

For each sub-domain a BFR belongs to, if it can act as an ingress or an egress router, it must be provisioned with a BFR-id that is unique within that sub-domain. A BFR-id is a small unstructured positive integer, and a sub-domain with 1,374 BFRs could hand out identifiers in the range 1 to 1,374. A router that belongs to more than one sub-domain may have a different identifier in each.

Each BFR must also be assigned a single BFR-prefix for each sub-domain it belongs to. The prefix must be an IP address, IPv4 or IPv6, of the BFR, and it is recommended that it be a loopback address. All prefixes used within one sub-domain must belong to the same address family, and the prefix must be routable in that sub-domain through the routing underlay associated with the sub-domain.

A BFR Identifier is a number in the range 1 to 65535. Within a sub-domain, every BFR that may act as an ingress or egress router must have a single identifier that identifies it uniquely there, while a router that never needs to be either does not need one. The value 0 is not a legal identifier. Assigning identifiers is outside the scope of the document, but the RFC recommends assigning them densely from the numbering space so that the encoding is efficient: with 256 or fewer egress routers, all identifiers should come from the range 1 to 256; with more than 256 but fewer than 512, from the range 1 to 512 with as few holes as possible in the earlier range.

Some deployments cannot support the full range of 65,535 identifiers. If the routers in a sub-domain support only 16 Set Identifiers and only BitStringLengths of 256 or less, then only 16 times 256, which is 4,096, identifiers can be supported there.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router in a BIER domain gets a number, unique inside its sub-domain, and an IP address that the rest of the domain can reach. The number is what appears in the packet; the address is what the routers use to send the packet to each other.

sections.title: Encoding Identifiers as Bits
sections.content:
To put a BFR-id into a packet, it has to be split into a Set Identifier and a BitString, and the split depends on the BitStringLength. If the identifier is N, the Set Identifier is the integer part of the quotient of N minus one divided by the BitStringLength, and the bit position that represents it is the remainder of that division plus one, counting from bit 1 at the low-order end.

Identifiers that resolve to the same Set Identifier can all be represented in a single BitString, and their bit strings are combined with a bitwise logical OR. That is what lets one bit string carry many destinations.

Every BFR must be provisioned with two things. It needs the BitStringLength and sub-domain to use when it imposes an encapsulation on a packet, called the Imposition BitStringLength and Imposition sub-domain. And it needs the BitStringLengths it will process when it receives packets, called the Disposition BitStringLengths. An ingress router is not required to use the same Imposition BitStringLength or sub-domain for every packet, but if it uses one for a given set of packets, the other routers with identifiers in that sub-domain should be provisioned to process packets of that length.

Every specification of a BIER encapsulation must define a default BitStringLength, and every router supporting it must be able to be provisioned with that default as its Imposition BitStringLength and as one of its Disposition BitStringLengths. A router must support Set Identifier values in the range 0 to 15, and may support values in the range 0 to 255. The total number of identifiers a router can represent is the BitStringLength multiplied by the number of Set Identifiers it supports: a deployment with a BitStringLength of 64 and 256 Set Identifiers can support 16,384 identifiers, and even a deployment supporting 256 Set Identifiers cannot support 65,535 identifiers unless the BitStringLength is at least 256.

When an ingress router knows the set of destinations, it partitions that set into subsets whose identifiers all resolve to the same Set Identifier, and makes one copy of the packet for each subset. The example in the RFC covers destinations numbered 27, 235 and 497 with a BitStringLength of 256: two copies are needed, one with a Set Identifier of 0 and bits 27 and 235 set, and one with a Set Identifier of 1 and bit 241 set.

Assigning identifiers densely is recommended because it minimises the number of Set Identifiers, and therefore the number of copies of a packet that have to be made. But other schemes can be better for a particular deployment. If every flow in a network is meant for the east coast or the west coast but not both, it pays to assign identifiers so that all the west coast routers fall in one Set Identifier subset and all the east coast routers in another.
sections.plainLanguage: A router number is too large to fit in one packet field, so it is divided into two parts: which block of numbers it falls in, and which bit inside that block. One packet can only describe one block, so destinations in a second block need a second copy of the packet.

sections.title: The Three Layers of BIER
sections.content:
It helps to think of BIER as three layers. The routing underlay establishes adjacencies between pairs of BFRs and determines one or more best paths from a given BFR to a given set of BFRs. Each path is a sequence of BFRs in which each is adjacent to the next. The underlay maps every BFR address to a set of one or more equal-cost adjacencies, and a BIER packet forwarded towards a given egress router follows the path the underlay selected for that router.

In a typical deployment the routing underlay is the default topology the Interior Gateway Protocol uses for unicast routing, so the underlay adjacencies are simply the OSPF adjacencies and a BIER packet follows the path OSPF chose for unicast traffic. If multicast traffic should follow a different path, a different underlay can be used: with multi-topology OSPF, one topology can serve unicast and the other multicast, and a routing underlay that builds a multicast-specific tree is another option, with BIER forwarding packets along that tree while unicast packets follow the ordinary best path. It is even possible to use several underlays, as long as the encapsulation lets a receiver infer which one a packet is using. Each BIER sub-domain must be associated with a single routing underlay, and by default each sub-domain uses the default topology of the unicast IGP. Where External BGP is used as the IGP, the underlay adjacencies are by default the BGP adjacencies.

The BIER layer is the set of protocols and procedures that carry a multicast data packet across the domain from its ingress router to its egress routers. It covers the procedures a router uses to advertise its BFR-prefix, its BFR-id in each sub-domain, the set of Disposition BitStringLengths it has been provisioned with, and optionally information about the routing underlay for each sub-domain. It also covers the procedures for imposing a BIER header on a packet, for forwarding and modifying BIER-encapsulated packets in transit, and for decapsulating a packet and dispatching it at the egress router.

The multicast flow overlay is the set of protocols and procedures that answer two questions: which egress routers should receive a packet that has just arrived from outside the domain, and how should a packet be dispatched once it has arrived at an egress router from inside the domain. Multicast VPN is one example. When the ingress and egress routers are provider edge routers providing a Multicast Virtual Private Network service, the overlay is the signalling described in RFC 6513 and RFC 6514, which lets an ingress router determine the set of egress routers for a flow and lets an egress router determine the virtual routing and forwarding tables the packets belong to. Because BIER is in effect a new kind of tunnelling technology, the MVPN signalling needs extensions to interface with the BIER layer, and those are specified separately. Other overlays may exist, and an overlay could also be implemented by a software-defined network controller.
sections.plainLanguage: BIER is built on top of ordinary IP routing. The underlay decides which way packets go, BIER adds the header that says which routers should get a copy, and a signalling layer above works out who actually wants the traffic.

sections.title: The Bit Index Routing and Forwarding Tables
sections.content:
The Bit Index Routing Table maps the BFR-id of an egress router in a sub-domain to that router's BFR-prefix and to the BFR neighbour on the path to it. The BFR neighbours of a router are the routers that the routing underlay says are its adjacencies, and each has a BFR-prefix of its own. When a BIER packet arrives, the receiving router learns the sub-domain and the destination identifiers from the encapsulation, and from the advertised information it finds each destination's prefix. The routing underlay then gives the IP address of the next hop on the path to that destination, and the prefix of that next hop is the neighbour. If the underlay offers several equal-cost paths, the router may have several neighbours for one destination.

The Bit Index Forwarding Table is derived from the routing table. Where several rows share the same Set Identifier and the same neighbour, the bit strings of those rows are combined with a bitwise OR to give a Forwarding Bit Mask for that combination of Set Identifier and neighbour. In the worked example in the RFC, two rows share a Set Identifier of 0 and a neighbour of C, and their masks, 0001 and 0010, combine into 0011. The forwarding table maps each destination identifier to its mask and its neighbour, and it is programmed into the data plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps two tables. One says which neighbouring router leads towards each possible destination. The other groups those destinations that share a neighbour into a single bit mask, so that one lookup can serve a whole group.

sections.title: The BIER Forwarding Procedure
sections.content:
The forwarding procedure is stated as a set of rules. First determine the packet's Set Identifier, BitStringLength and sub-domain. If the BitString is entirely zeroes, discard the packet, because forwarding is complete. Otherwise find the position k of the rightmost bit that is set. If bit k identifies the router itself, copy the packet and send the copy to the multicast flow overlay, then clear bit k in the original and start again. Otherwise use k, with the Set Identifier, sub-domain and BitStringLength, as an index into the forwarding table to extract the Forwarding Bit Mask and the neighbour. Copy the packet, AND the copy's BitString with the mask, and send it to that neighbour; if the neighbour is the null next hop the copy is discarded. Then AND the original packet's BitString with the inverse of the mask, which clears the bits that have just been dealt with, and start again.

The point of this procedure is that the packet is forwarded to a given neighbour only once, and the number of forwarding table lookups equals the number of neighbours the packet must be sent to rather than the number of destinations. Only the bits belonging to the destinations reached through that neighbour stay set in the copy that is sent to it.

Other parts of the header need attention as well. A TTL field in the BIER header has to be decremented as the packet travels. The BIFT-id field implicitly identifies a Set Identifier, a sub-domain and a BitStringLength, so when a packet is sent to a neighbour its BIFT-id must be changed to the value that neighbour advertised for the same three things, which in the MPLS encapsulation amounts to a label swap. If the neighbour is connected over several parallel links, an entropy field in the encapsulation should be respected so that two packets with the same entropy value take the same interface. Where the underlay offers several equal-cost paths, the procedures have to be augmented to support load balancing. And where unicast traffic to a neighbour goes through a bypass tunnel, the multicast traffic should go through the same tunnel, so that fast reroute schemes apply to multicast as well.

Duplicate delivery is impossible by construction. When a packet is replicated, no two copies have a destination in common, and a router that forwards a packet further first clears the bit identifying itself. As long as the routing underlay gives loop-free paths, BIER packets do not loop, and because the BIER layer creates no paths of its own no extra loop-prevention is needed. If the underlay is not loop free, packets may loop, but they will never be delivered twice to the same router. These properties remove the need for the Reverse Path Forwarding check used in conventional IP multicast forwarding.

The RFC also covers the case where some routers in the domain do not support BIER. Taking the underlay's shortest-path tree rooted at a BIER router, a child that does not support BIER is removed and its children are re-parented onto the router, which then reaches them through a unicast tunnel. A simpler variant re-parents the destinations reached through the non-BIER child instead, which is easier because the set of such destinations can be read from the forwarding table, but is less optimal because packets are then unicast directly to those destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: To forward a packet, a router takes the lowest bit that is still set, looks up which neighbour leads towards it, copies the packet with only that neighbour's destinations left in it, and sends it. It then clears those bits and repeats. Because each copy carries only its own destinations, no router can ever receive the same packet twice.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
BIER offers a radical simplification over current IP multicast operations: no tree-building control plane, no per-flow forwarding state, no Reverse Path Forwarding, no Rendezvous Point. Forwarding and replication follow the unicast paths to each bit position set in the packet, so an encapsulated multicast packet takes the same path as unicast to each set bit, from the entry point of the domain to the edge device that holds that bit. The BIER forwarding table can be derived from the shortest-path unicast forwarding table, or from any other path calculation in or out of band.

Because of these differences, operational expectations from traditional multicast solutions do not apply. There is no granular per-flow state at each node defining a tree, and monitoring flows at the forwarding-plane level is not provided in a BIER node. Packet counters may be kept for identifiers or for next-hop neighbours, and any flow-based metric would require deeper packet inspection, which is outside the scope of the document. In this way BIER is more like unicast.

The reduction in state is what allows the key operational benefit, deterministic convergence: the BIER forwarding table can converge immediately after the unicast forwarding table, regardless of how many multicast flows are crossing the links. Careful monitoring of flow utilisation is not required inside a BIER domain.

Configuration follows from this. A BIER domain requires that each edge router be given a unique bit position, its BFR-id, configured on that router and associated with a unique IP address of it. The association must also be advertised into the IGP of the domain, either implied by the BIER configuration or by IGP-specific configuration, and existing manual or automated configuration tools must be able to reach BIER-specific settings. The document does not dictate a configuration method.
sections.plainLanguage: Because nothing in the middle tracks the flows, the forwarding table can settle as soon as the ordinary routing table does. There is also no per-flow monitoring to build, which makes the system behave more like unicast than like classic multicast.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BIER inherits the security considerations of the multicast flow overlay it is paired with, and of the routing underlay it is paired with.

If the encapsulation of a packet specifies a Set Identifier or a BitString other than the one the ingress router intended, the packet is likely to be misdelivered. If the encapsulation is modified, whether by error or by an attacker, in a way not specified in the document, the packet may be misdelivered. Some modifications, for example setting every bit in the BitString, result in deliberate or accidental denial-of-service attacks. A compromised ingress router can do exactly that by imposing an encapsulation with all bits set.

Every BFR must be provisioned to know which of its interfaces lead into a BIER domain and which do not, and BIER-encapsulated packets must not be accepted from outside the domain, since an attacker could set all the bits and flood the domain. If two interfaces lead to different BIER domains, the BFR must be provisioned to know that, or packets from one domain may leak into another, which is likely to cause misdelivery. Incorrect provisioning of the routers can also lead to denial-of-service attacks. And if the procedures used to advertise identifiers and prefixes are not secure, an attack on them can result in incorrect delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the attack surface. A packet whose bits are all set asks every router in the domain to copy it, so BIER packets must never be accepted from outside the domain, and the routers must know which of their links belong to which domain.

items.title: BFR-id
items.text: A number in the range 1 to 65535 that identifies a router inside one sub-domain.

items.title: Set Identifier
items.text: Which block of the numbering space the identifier falls in.

items.title: BitStringLength
items.text: How many bits one block holds, for example 256.

items.title: BitString
items.text: One bit per router in the block. A set bit means that router must receive the packet.

items.title: Why the Set Identifier matters
items.text: A packet carries one Set Identifier at a time, so routers in a second block need a second copy of the packet.
